summary: Gives an analysis of one method of choosing among equal-cost paths in equal-cost multi-path routing.

eli5.summary: When several paths are equally good, a router needs a fair way to pick. This examines one such way.

questions: how much disruption does hash threshold cause
how does ecmp choose a next hop
subtitle: A closer look at hash-threshold, a way for routers to spread flows over equal-cost paths while disturbing few of them when paths change.

tldr.problem: A router using equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) must choose a next hop per packet, and the choice should be cheap and should not shuffle many flows onto new paths when the set of next hops changes.
tldr.mechanism: Hash-threshold hashes the flow's header fields into a key and gives each of the N next hops an equal region of the key space. A single division finds the region, and the analysis shows that removing or adding a next hop moves between 1/4 and 1/2 of flows.
tldr.outcome: It is as fast as modulo-N and less disruptive. Highest random weight (HRW) disrupts less (1/N) but costs more, so it fits when per-flow state is kept.

today: RFC 2992 is an Informational memo from November 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a companion to RFC 2991.

sections.title: The Hash-Threshold Method
sections.content:
In hash-threshold the router first computes a key by hashing (for example with CRC16) the packet header fields that identify a flow, such as the source and destination fields. The N next hops have been assigned unique regions in the key space, and the region that contains the key decides which next hop is used.

The RFC gives an example. With a CRC16 the key space is 16 bits, and with 4 next hops each region is 65536/4, or 16k, large. The next hop is the one whose region contains the CRC result.
sections.eli5: Give each trip a number, cut the number line into equal slices, and send the trip down whichever road owns the slice with its number.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content:
The analysis assumes regions of equal size. If the hash output is uniform, flows spread evenly across paths. Unequal-cost multi-path routing could be done with regions of unequal size, but it is out of scope.

Cost has three parts: choosing the regions, computing the key and comparing the key to the regions. The algorithm does not specify the hash function, so that cost is the hash function's own cost, and the memo suggests it could run in hardware in parallel with other work. With equal regions, boundaries are trivial and need not be stored. Finding the region is a division:

regionsize = keyspace.size / #{nexthops}
region = key / regionsize;

Keeping the next hops in an array indexed by region gives a lookup time of O(1).
sections.eli5: Finding the right slice is one quick division, like working out which box a number falls in. It takes the same time no matter how many roads there are.

sections.title: Disruption When Next Hops Change
sections.content:
Disruption is the fraction of total flows whose path changes after some change in the router. It matters because protocols such as TCP work better when the path does not change, and it becomes important if a path is flapping. Round-robin is disruptive even when nothing changes, but hash-threshold keeps the same next hop for a flow as long as the region boundaries stay put. With equal-sized regions, boundaries move only when a next hop is added or removed, and then all regions grow or shrink to fill the key space.

The RFC works through examples with five regions. Deleting region 3 gives a total disruption of 3/10, and deleting region 4 gives 7/20. Adding a region disrupts the same fraction of flows as removing one.

In general, the disruption when removing region K of N is (K-1)(K) + (N-K)(N-K+1) all over 2(N)(N-1). It is smallest when K is as close as possible to halfway between 1 and N, where it works out to 1/4 + 1/(4*N), and largest when an edge region (1 or N) is removed, where it is 1/2. The range is therefore (1/4, 1/2], and the RFC recommends adding new regions to the center rather than the ends.
sections.eli5: When a slice disappears, the neighbors stretch to fill the gap and the slices shift. Trips near the shifted edges change roads. If the lost slice is in the middle, the fewest trips are affected.

sections.title: Comparison to Other Algorithms
sections.content:
The comparison covers only methods that are not disruptive by design, which rules out round-robin and random choice. That leaves modulo-N and highest random weight (HRW).

  • Modulo-N: hash the flow fields and apply a final modulo-N. Its performance equals hash-threshold, but it is the most disruptive: adding or removing a next hop disrupts (N-1)/N of flows.
  • HRW: for each next hop, seed a pseudo-random number generator with the flow fields and the next hop to get a weight, then pick the highest. Disruption is minimal, always 1/N, but selection is more expensive.

Hash-threshold and modulo-N look up in O(1); HRW is O(N). All three need a hash of the flow fields, so the hash cost can be set aside unless it cannot be done cheaply. The RFC suggests considering HRW when its cost is acceptable, for example when per-flow state is kept so the choice is made infrequently. When HRW is too expensive, hash-threshold is the obvious choice since it performs as well as modulo-N and is less disruptive. See RFC 2991 for the wider discussion.
sections.eli5: The quick shuffle (modulo-N) is as fast as slices but moves almost everyone. The bidding method (HRW) moves the fewest but is slow. Slices are the happy middle.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document is an analysis of an algorithm used to implement an ECMP routing decision, and it says this analysis does not directly affect the security of the Internet infrastructure. It raises no further security issues.
sections.eli5: This is just a study of how to pick a road, so it does not create any new security worries on its own.
